claim: Hantaviruses are RNA viruses with known epidemic threat and potential for emergence.
source: Hantaviruses are RNA viruses with known epidemic threat and potential for emergence.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about hantaviruses and their classification.

claim: Several rodent-borne hantaviruses cause zoonoses accompanied by severe illness and death.
source: Several rodent-borne hantaviruses cause zoonoses accompanied by severe illness and death.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and consensus about hantavirus disease.

claim: β3/β1-containing integrins have been presumed to be the major hantavirus entry receptors.
source: Despite the long-standing presumption that β3/β1-containing integrins are the major hantavirus entry receptors, rigorous genetic loss-of-function evidence supporting their requirement, and that of decay-accelerating factor (DAF), is lacking.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and represents the historical scientific understanding.

claim: Rigorous genetic loss-of-function evidence supporting the requirement of β3/β1-containing integrins and DAF for hantavirus entry is lacking.
source: Despite the long-standing presumption that β3/β1-containing integrins are the major hantavirus entry receptors, rigorous genetic loss-of-function evidence supporting their requirement, and that of decay-accelerating factor (DAF), is lacking.
evidence: This is an inference based on review of existing literature and represents a gap in knowledge.

claim: The loss of β3 integrin, β1 integrin, and/or DAF had little or no effect on entry by a large panel of hantaviruses.
source: The loss of β3 integrin, β1 integrin, and/or DAF had little or no effect on entry by a large panel of hantaviruses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from knockout studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of protocadherin-1 substantially reduced hantavirus entry and infection.
source: By contrast, loss of protocadherin-1, a recently identified entry receptor for some hantaviruses, substantially reduced hantavirus entry and infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from knockout studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: Major host molecules necessary for endothelial cell entry by PCDH1-independent hantaviruses remain to be discovered.
source: We conclude that major host molecules necessary for endothelial cell entry by PCDH1-independent hantaviruses remain to be discovered.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that known receptors are not required.

claim: Hantaviruses are enveloped viruses with segmented negative-strand RNA genomes.
source: Hantaviruses are a large family of enveloped viruses with segmented negative-strand RNA genomes whose members infect a wide range of mammalian hosts (Elliott et al., 1991; Mittler et al., 2019; Vaheri et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: Hantaviruses infect a wide range of mammalian hosts.
source: Hantaviruses are a large family of enveloped viruses with segmented negative-strand RNA genomes whose members infect a wide range of mammalian hosts (Elliott et al., 1991; Mittler et al., 2019; Vaheri et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Zoonotic transmission of some rodent-borne hantaviruses is associated with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS).
source: The zoonotic transmission of some rodent-borne hantaviruses is associated with two major diseases in humans, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), in endemic regions of Europe/Asia and North/South America, respectively (Peters et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: HFRS occurs in endemic regions of Europe/Asia.
source: The zoonotic transmission of some rodent-borne hantaviruses is associated with two major diseases in humans, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), in endemic regions of Europe/Asia and North/South America, respectively (Peters et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: HCPS occurs in endemic regions of North/South America.
source: The zoonotic transmission of some rodent-borne hantaviruses is associated with two major diseases in humans, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), in endemic regions of Europe/Asia and North/South America, respectively (Peters et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Zoonotic infections by Seoul virus (SEOV) have a global distribution mirroring that of their rodent hosts.
source: Zoonotic infections by some other hantaviruses (e.g., Seoul virus, SEOV) have a global distribution mirroring that of their rodent hosts.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about SEOV distribution.

claim: Most HFRS cases are associated with Hantaan virus (HTNV), SEOV, Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV), and Puumala virus (PUUV) infections.
source: Most HFRS cases are associated with the 'Old-World hantaviruses' Hantaan virus (HTNV), SEOV, Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV), and Puumala virus (PUUV) infections, whereas HCPS is primarily caused by the 'New-World hantaviruses' Andes virus (ANDV) and Sin Nombre virus (SNV) (Jiang et al., 2016; Macneil et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HCPS is primarily caused by Andes virus (ANDV) and Sin Nombre virus (SNV).
source: Most HFRS cases are associated with the 'Old-World hantaviruses' Hantaan virus (HTNV), SEOV, Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV), and Puumala virus (PUUV) infections, whereas HCPS is primarily caused by the 'New-World hantaviruses' Andes virus (ANDV) and Sin Nombre virus (SNV) (Jiang et al., 2016; Macneil et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Humans are typically dead-end hosts for rodent-borne hantaviruses.
source: Although humans are typically dead-end hosts for rodent-borne hantaviruses, several incidents of ANDV person-to-person transmission, including a recent superspreader event, have been documented, underscoring the epidemic threat posed by these agents (Martínez et al., 2020; Padula et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and established knowledge.

claim: Several incidents of ANDV person-to-person transmission have been documented.
source: Although humans are typically dead-end hosts for rodent-borne hantaviruses, several incidents of ANDV person-to-person transmission, including a recent superspreader event, have been documented, underscoring the epidemic threat posed by these agents (Martínez et al., 2020; Padula et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A recent ANDV superspreader event has been documented.
source: Although humans are typically dead-end hosts for rodent-borne hantaviruses, several incidents of ANDV person-to-person transmission, including a recent superspreader event, have been documented, underscoring the epidemic threat posed by these agents (Martínez et al., 2020; Padula et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: No FDA-approved vaccines or specific therapeutics are available for hantaviruses.
source: Despite this strong potential for transmission from known and unknown host reservoirs and the significant burden of severe disease, no FDA-approved vaccines or specific therapeutics are available for hantaviruses (Mittler et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and represents current knowledge.

claim: Integrins (αVβ3, α5β1, αMβ2, and αXβ2) have been previously proposed as candidate hantavirus receptors and/or entry factors.
source: Integrins (αVβ3, α5β1, αMβ2, and αXβ2) and components of the complement system (e.g., decay-accelerating factor [DAF]) have been previously proposed as candidate hantavirus receptors and/or entry factors, based largely on cDNA complementation experiments to rescue infection in nonpermissive cell lines, receptor-blocking studies in non-polarized and polarized endothelial cells and/or binding assays (Buranda et al., 2010; Gavrilovskaya et al., 1999; Gavrilovskaya et al., 1998; Krautkrämer and Zeier, 2008; Popugaeva et al., 2012; Raftery et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Decay-accelerating factor (DAF) has been previously proposed as a candidate hantavirus receptor and/or entry factor.
source: Integrins (αVβ3, α5β1, αMβ2, and αXβ2) and components of the complement system (e.g., decay-accelerating factor [DAF]) have been previously proposed as candidate hantavirus receptors and/or entry factors, based largely on cDNA complementation experiments to rescue infection in nonpermissive cell lines, receptor-blocking studies in non-polarized and polarized endothelial cells and/or binding assays (Buranda et al., 2010; Gavrilovskaya et al., 1999; Gavrilovskaya et al., 1998; Krautkrämer and Zeier, 2008; Popugaeva et al., 2012; Raftery et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: β3- and β1-containing integrins have been presumed to be the major entry receptors for virulent and avirulent hantaviruses, respectively, for over two decades.
source: β3- and β1-containing integrins have been presumed to be the major entry receptors for virulent and avirulent hantaviruses, respectively, for over two decades (Gavrilovskaya et al., 1999; Gavrilovskaya et al., 2002; Gavrilovskaya et al., 1998; Raymond et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) is a critical determinant of attachment, entry, and infection by New-World hantaviruses in primary human microvascular endothelial cells.
source: More recently, we identified protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) as a critical determinant of attachment, entry, and infection by New-World hantaviruses, but not their Old-World counterparts, in primary human microvascular endothelial cells (Jangra et al., 2018), which are major targets of hantavirus infection in vivo (Mackow and Gavrilovskaya, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: PCDH1 is not a critical determinant of attachment, entry, and infection by Old-World hantaviruses in primary human microvascular endothelial cells.
source: More recently, we identified protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) as a critical determinant of attachment, entry, and infection by New-World hantaviruses, but not their Old-World counterparts, in primary human microvascular endothelial cells (Jangra et al., 2018), which are major targets of hantavirus infection in vivo (Mackow and Gavrilovskaya, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Primary human microvascular endothelial cells are major targets of hantavirus infection in vivo.
source: More recently, we identified protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) as a critical determinant of attachment, entry, and infection by New-World hantaviruses, but not their Old-World counterparts, in primary human microvascular endothelial cells (Jangra et al., 2018), which are major targets of hantavirus infection in vivo (Mackow and Gavrilovskaya, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: PCDH1 was identified in a comprehensive genetic screen for ANDV entry factors.
source: PCDH1 was identified in a comprehensive genetic screen for ANDV entry factors, and its genetic depletion in endothelial cells inhibited viral entry and infection.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (implicitly referenced).

claim: Genetic depletion of PCDH1 in endothelial cells inhibited viral entry and infection.
source: PCDH1 was identified in a comprehensive genetic screen for ANDV entry factors, and its genetic depletion in endothelial cells inhibited viral entry and infection.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (implicitly referenced).

claim: Genetic loss of PCDH1 reduced viral multiplication in Syrian hamsters.
source: Further, genetic loss of PCDH1 reduced viral multiplication in Syrian hamsters and protected them from lethal HCPS-like disease (Jangra et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Genetic loss of PCDH1 protected Syrian hamsters from lethal HCPS-like disease.
source: Further, genetic loss of PCDH1 reduced viral multiplication in Syrian hamsters and protected them from lethal HCPS-like disease (Jangra et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: None of the candidate receptors (other than PCDH1) were observed as hits in two independently conducted, unbiased genetic screens for hantavirus host factors.
source: By contrast, none of the other candidate receptors were observed as hits in two independently conducted, unbiased genetic screens for hantavirus host factors (Jangra et al., 2018; Kleinfelter et al., 2015; Petersen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The candidate receptors (β3 integrin, β1 integrin, DAF) have not been rigorously evaluated for their genetic requirement in physiologically relevant in vitro and in vivo models.
source: Moreover, to our knowledge, they have not been rigorously evaluated for their genetic requirement in physiologically relevant in vitro and in vivo models.
evidence: This is an inference based on review of existing literature.

claim: The critical host determinants of hantavirus entry remain incompletely defined.
source: To date, therefore, the critical host determinants of hantavirus entry remain incompletely defined.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gaps in knowledge identified.

claim: TIME cells are a previously well-characterized human microvascular endothelial cell line.
source: We first selected a previously well-characterized human microvascular endothelial cell line, TIME, as a biologically faithful and genetically manipulable model for primary endothelial cells (Venetsanakos et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: TIME cells resemble primary human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC) in expressing key endothelial markers PECAM-1/CD31 and von Willebrand factor (vWF).
source: We confirmed through cell staining and flow cytometry that this cell line resembled primary human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC) in expressing key endothelial markers – the platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule-1 (PECAM-1/CD31) and the von Willebrand factor (vWF) – as well as the four candidate hantavirus receptors under investigation (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: TIME cells express the four candidate hantavirus receptors under investigation (PCDH1, β3 integrin, β1 integrin, DAF).
source: We confirmed through cell staining and flow cytometry that this cell line resembled primary human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC) in expressing key endothelial markers – the platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule-1 (PECAM-1/CD31) and the von Willebrand factor (vWF) – as well as the four candidate hantavirus receptors under investigation (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: TIME cells are susceptible to hantavirus entry mediated by divergent Gn/Gc proteins.
source: Furthermore, TIME cells were susceptible to hantavirus entry mediated by divergent Gn/Gc proteins (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: TIME cells are suitable to study the virus–host interactions that drive hantavirus entry in endothelial cells.
source: We concluded, therefore, that TIME cells were also suitable to study the virus–host interactions that drive hantavirus entry in endothelial cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental characterization of TIME cells.

claim: PCDH1 KO substantially diminished ANDV and SNV Gn/Gc-mediated infection.
source: PCDH1 KO substantially diminished ANDV and SNV Gn/Gc-mediated infection, whereas it had no discernible effect on that by HTNV Gn/Gc.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from knockout studies.

claim: PCDH1 KO had no discernible effect on HTNV Gn/Gc-mediated infection.
source: PCDH1 KO substantially diminished ANDV and SNV Gn/Gc-mediated infection, whereas it had no discernible effect on that by HTNV Gn/Gc.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from knockout studies.

claim: ITGB3 and DAF KOs did not inhibit endothelial cell entry mediated by ANDV, SNV, and HTNV glycoproteins.
source: Unexpectedly, ITGB3 and DAF KOs did not inhibit endothelial cell entry mediated by these glycoproteins (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: Loss of PCDH1 substantially reduced endothelial cell entry and infection mediated by the glycoproteins from New-World hantaviruses (CHOV, MPRLV, PHV).
source: Loss of PCDH1 substantially reduced endothelial cell entry and infection mediated by the glycoproteins from the New-World viruses but not the Old-World viruses, in a manner that could be restored by complementation with PCDH1 cDNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from knockout and complementation studies.

claim: Loss of PCDH1 did not substantially reduce endothelial cell entry and infection mediated by the glycoproteins from Old-World hantaviruses (PUUV, SEOV, DOBV).
source: Loss of PCDH1 substantially reduced endothelial cell entry and infection mediated by the glycoproteins from the New-World viruses but not the Old-World viruses, in a manner that could be restored by complementation with PCDH1 cDNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from knockout studies.

claim: The effect of PCDH1 loss on New-World hantavirus entry could be restored by complementation with PCDH1 cDNA.
source: Loss of PCDH1 substantially reduced endothelial cell entry and infection mediated by the glycoproteins from the New-World viruses but not the Old-World viruses, in a manner that could be restored by complementation with PCDH1 cDNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from complementation studies.

claim: None of the tested hantaviruses (CHOV, MPRLV, PHV, PUUV, SEOV, DOBV) displayed a requirement for ITGB3 or DAF.
source: By contrast, and as observed above for ANDV, SNV, and HTNV, none of these viruses displayed a requirement for ITGB3 or DAF (Figures 1c–2c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1c-2c.

claim: PCDH1/ITGB3 and PCDH1/DAF1 KO cells resembled PCDH1 KO cells in susceptibility to rVSV-Gn/Gc infection.
source: PCDH1/ITGB3 and PCDH1/DAF1 KO cells resembled PCDH1 KO cells in susceptibility to rVSV-Gn/Gc infection (Figure 2d), indicating that the loss of PCDH1 did not unmask viral requirements for β3 integrin or DAF, or vice versa.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The loss of PCDH1 did not unmask viral requirements for β3 integrin or DAF.
source: PCDH1/ITGB3 and PCDH1/DAF1 KO cells resembled PCDH1 KO cells in susceptibility to rVSV-Gn/Gc infection (Figure 2d), indicating that the loss of PCDH1 did not unmask viral requirements for β3 integrin or DAF, or vice versa.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data from double knockout studies.

claim: ITGB3/DAF KO cells remained fully susceptible to viral entry by ANDV and SNV.
source: Furthermore, ITGB3/DAF KO cells remained fully susceptible to viral entry (ANDV, SNV) or exhibited only a modest (~25%) reduction (HTNV) (Figure 2d), suggesting that the lack of viral entry phenotypes in the ITGB3 and DAF single-KO cells cannot be explained by the functional redundancy of these two proteins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: ITGB3/DAF KO cells exhibited only a modest (~25%) reduction in HTNV entry.
source: Furthermore, ITGB3/DAF KO cells remained fully susceptible to viral entry (ANDV, SNV) or exhibited only a modest (~25%) reduction (HTNV) (Figure 2d), suggesting that the lack of viral entry phenotypes in the ITGB3 and DAF single-KO cells cannot be explained by the functional redundancy of these two proteins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The lack of viral entry phenotypes in the ITGB3 and DAF single-KO cells cannot be explained by the functional redundancy of these two proteins.
source: Furthermore, ITGB3/DAF KO cells remained fully susceptible to viral entry (ANDV, SNV) or exhibited only a modest (~25%) reduction (HTNV) (Figure 2d), suggesting that the lack of viral entry phenotypes in the ITGB3 and DAF single-KO cells cannot be explained by the functional redundancy of these two proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data from double knockout studies.

claim: PCDH1 plays a critical role in endothelial cell infection by the New-World hantaviruses ANDV, SNV, and PHV.
source: These experiments independently corroborated our results with rVSVs. Specifically, we observed a critical role for PCDH1 in endothelial cell infection by the New-World hantaviruses ANDV, SNV, and PHV, and no apparent roles for β3 integrin and DAF in entry by virulent New-World and Old-World hantaviruses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from authentic hantavirus infections.

claim: β3 integrin and DAF have no apparent roles in entry by virulent New-World and Old-World hantaviruses.
source: These experiments independently corroborated our results with rVSVs. Specifically, we observed a critical role for PCDH1 in endothelial cell infection by the New-World hantaviruses ANDV, SNV, and PHV, and no apparent roles for β3 integrin and DAF in entry by virulent New-World and Old-World hantaviruses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from authentic hantavirus infections.

claim: Quantitative real-time PCR revealed a substantial reduction in the generation of SNV progeny genomes at 24 hr post-infection in cells deficient for PCDH1 (5 ± 2%).
source: Concordantly, quantitative real-time PCR revealed a substantial reduction in the generation of SNV progeny genomes at 24 hr post-infection in cells deficient for PCDH1 (5 ± 2%) but not β3 integrin (108 ± 15%) or DAF (82 ± 13%; mean ± SEM, n=6 from two independent experiments for each cell line).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from qPCR measurements.

claim: Quantitative real-time PCR revealed no substantial reduction in the generation of SNV progeny genomes at 24 hr post-infection in cells deficient for β3 integrin (108 ± 15%).
source: Concordantly, quantitative real-time PCR revealed a substantial reduction in the generation of SNV progeny genomes at 24 hr post-infection in cells deficient for PCDH1 (5 ± 2%) but not β3 integrin (108 ± 15%) or DAF (82 ± 13%; mean ± SEM, n=6 from two independent experiments for each cell line).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from qPCR measurements.

claim: Quantitative real-time PCR revealed no substantial reduction in the generation of SNV progeny genomes at 24 hr post-infection in cells deficient for DAF (82 ± 13%).
source: Concordantly, quantitative real-time PCR revealed a substantial reduction in the generation of SNV progeny genomes at 24 hr post-infection in cells deficient for PCDH1 (5 ± 2%) but not β3 integrin (108 ± 15%) or DAF (82 ± 13%; mean ± SEM, n=6 from two independent experiments for each cell line).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from qPCR measurements.

claim: β1 integrin has been hypothesized as a receptor for avirulent hantaviruses.
source: Contrary to earlier hypotheses suggesting β1 integrin as receptors for avirulent hantaviruses (Gavrilovskaya et al., 1998), we also found no apparent role for β1 integrin in entry by both the rVSV and the authentic version of New-World hantavirus PHV (Figure 2e, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: β1 integrin has no apparent role in entry by the rVSV and authentic version of New-World hantavirus PHV.
source: Contrary to earlier hypotheses suggesting β1 integrin as receptors for avirulent hantaviruses (Gavrilovskaya et al., 1998), we also found no apparent role for β1 integrin in entry by both the rVSV and the authentic version of New-World hantavirus PHV (Figure 2e, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Endothelial cells are primary targets of viral infection central to hantavirus disease in humans.
source: Endothelial cells are primary targets of the viral infection and subversion that is central to hantavirus disease in humans.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Only the genetic loss of PCDH1 was associated with the reduction of viral infection in endothelial cells among the major receptor/entry host factor candidates (β3 integrin, β1 integrin, DAF, PCDH1).
source: Of the major receptor/entry host factor candidates proposed to date for hantaviruses (β3 integrin, β1 integrin, DAF, PCDH1), only the genetic loss of PCDH1 was associated with the reduction of viral infection in endothelial cells in this study, underscoring PCDH1's critical role as an entry receptor for New-World hantaviruses, but not their Old-World counterparts in these cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The previously described candidate receptors (β3 integrin, β1 integrin, DAF) are dispensable for viral entry in endothelial cells.
source: We conclude that the other previously described candidate receptors (β3 integrin, β1 integrin, DAF) are dispensable for viral entry in endothelial cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data from the study.

claim: The results do not rule out that β3 integrin, β1 integrin, or DAF is involved in hantavirus entry into other cell types not examined in this study.
source: We note that our results do not rule out that one or more of these proteins is involved in (1) hantavirus entry into other cell types not examined herein; (2) hantavirus entry into polarized cells, as proposed for DAF (Krautkrämer and Zeier, 2008); or (3) endothelial cell subversion post-viral entry, as shown previously (Gavrilovskaya et al., 1999; Gavrilovskaya et al., 1998; Krautkrämer and Zeier, 2008).
evidence: This is speculation about alternative roles not tested in the study.

claim: The results do not rule out that β3 integrin, β1 integrin, or DAF is involved in hantavirus entry into polarized cells.
source: We note that our results do not rule out that one or more of these proteins is involved in (1) hantavirus entry into other cell types not examined herein; (2) hantavirus entry into polarized cells, as proposed for DAF (Krautkrämer and Zeier, 2008); or (3) endothelial cell subversion post-viral entry, as shown previously (Gavrilovskaya et al., 1999; Gavrilovskaya et al., 1998; Krautkrämer and Zeier, 2008).
evidence: This is speculation about alternative roles not tested in the study, with citation to prior literature.

claim: The results do not rule out that β3 integrin, β1 integrin, or DAF is involved in endothelial cell subversion post-viral entry.
source: We note that our results do not rule out that one or more of these proteins is involved in (1) hantavirus entry into other cell types not examined herein; (2) hantavirus entry into polarized cells, as proposed for DAF (Krautkrämer and Zeier, 2008); or (3) endothelial cell subversion post-viral entry, as shown previously (Gavrilovskaya et al., 1999; Gavrilovskaya et al., 1998; Krautkrämer and Zeier, 2008).
evidence: This is speculation about alternative roles not tested in the study, with citation to prior literature.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 genome engineering was used to knockout PCDH1, DAF, ITGB3, and ITGB1 in TIME cells.
source: We used CRISPR/Cas9 genome engineering to knockout (KO) PCDH1, DAF, and the genes encoding β3 and β1 integrins (ITGB3 and ITGB1, respectively), in TIME cells.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used.

claim: Subpopulations of CRISPR/Cas9-engineered, receptor-deficient cells were isolated by FACS following staining of live cells with protein-specific antibodies.
source: Subpopulations of CRISPR/Cas9-engineered, receptor-deficient cells were isolated by FACS following staining of live cells with protein-specific antibodies.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used.

claim: Gene KO was verified by Sanger sequencing of PCR amplicons bearing the targeted genomic loci.
source: Gene KO was verified by Sanger sequencing of PCR amplicons bearing the targeted genomic loci (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 ).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used and is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of protein expression at the cell surface was verified by flow cytometry.
source: Loss of protein expression at the cell surface and in cell extracts was verified by flow cytometry and western blotting, respectively (Figure 1b,c).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used and is supported by data in Figure 1b,c.

claim: Loss of protein expression in cell extracts was verified by western blotting.
source: Loss of protein expression at the cell surface and in cell extracts was verified by flow cytometry and western blotting, respectively (Figure 1b,c).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used and is supported by data in Figure 1b,c.

claim: All sequenced clones from each KO cell population showed an indel at the targeted site, resulting in a frameshift that brought one or more stop codons into frame.
source: For each knockout cell population, 15–20 clones were subjected to Sanger sequencing. All sequenced clones showed an indel at the targeted site, resulting in a frameshift that brought one or more stop codons into frame.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
